chapters.n: Wear the mask long enough and it grows in
chapters.w: Necessary, but it has to come off
chapters.dek: What happens after years inside a role. Jung says the mask isn't the problem — here's where the problem is.
chapters.txt: Jung used the word mask for what a person puts on outside: the post, the identity, the version of you others expect. The mask is necessary; without it you can't deal with the world. The danger lies elsewhere — wear it long enough and you take it for yourself. Then every judgement starts from the role, and when the role is removed — retirement, redundancy, children leaving — whoever is left finds they don't know who to be. A mask isn't dishonesty. It's a necessary interface — The voice you use at work, the way you are with clients — masks, and they should exist. Jung isn't asking anyone to take theirs off. He's asking that you can tell them apart: which part the role requires and which part is yours. Telling them apart is what keeps it removable. The moment the role is taken is the moment you find out — Retirement, redundancy, children leaving are the same event: the mask removed from outside. How badly you panic then measures how much of what you built grew only on the role. The more complete the panic, the less the separating was ever done. Keep one area the role can't reach — In practice: hold on to something unrelated to your identity — an interest, a set of people who don't know your job title. Its usefulness isn't in how important it is but in not moving when the role does. It's what you're standing on when the role goes. Where you are: you've been in one role for years
q: The mask is necessary. The trouble is taking it for yourself.
What's left when the identity goes can't be seen in advance.

chapters.n: After losing to it, he changed the rules
chapters.w: Let people bring machines to the board
chapters.dek: When a machine wins at your craft, what's left of it. Why Kasparov invited the computer onto his own board.
chapters.txt: He beat Deep Blue in Philadelphia in 1996. In the New York rematch of May 1997 it beat him 3.5–2.5, the first time a world champion lost a formal match to a machine. A year later he staged an event in León under new rules: each side brought a computer to the board and could consult it at any time. He called it Advanced Chess. The reasoning was plain — calculation was already lost, so stop competing on who calculates faster. First identify what's no longer worth competing on — The day machines won on depth of calculation, the 'who sees furthest' track closed. Training on a closed track has no exit however hard you train. The first step isn't redoubling effort; it's striking the lost item off your own list of what you're worth. Change the rules, not the effort — He didn't train harder and he didn't switch fields. He changed what the contest permits. When a tool matches an ability, the valuable position moves to how the tool gets used — and somebody has to define that position before it exists. Inviting the tool in holds better than keeping it out — A contest that bans tools survives only on enforcement, and collapses the moment enforcement slips. A contest that permits them is measuring something else — something that doesn't expire as tools improve, because it improves alongside them. Where you are: a core skill in your field has been matched by a tool, and you're still training on the old track. Ask first: which item in
q: Calculation was already lost, so stop competing on calculation.
The first step isn't more effort. It's striking out what's lost.

chapters.n: The winner wasn't the best human or the best machine
chapters.w: It was the pair with the best process
chapters.dek: What human plus tool is actually good at. Why two amateurs won a tournament where everyone could use a computer.
chapters.txt: A freestyle online tournament in 2005 admitted grandmasters and supercomputers, with humans and machines free to team up. The winners were two American amateurs, Steven Cramton and Zackary Stephen, running three ordinary PCs. Their method was to ask all three and apply their own judgement only where the three disagreed. Kasparov later compressed it: a weak human plus a machine plus a good process beats a strong human plus a machine plus a poor one. The value moves from answering well to asking well — Where all three machines return the same answer, adding a person adds nothing. The human value concentrates entirely in the few moves where they disagree — finding the disagreement and judging which side to believe. That is a different job from playing chess. Process makes up for ability; ability can't make up for process — The amateurs won on a stable checking routine. The grandmasters lost by treating the machine as a reference and calling it themselves at the end. The first doesn't depend on how you feel that day; the second does. That is how weaker players beat stronger ones. Don't keep only one tool — With one machine there is no disagreement to look at — you either believe all of it or none of it. Three aren't valuable because the compute adds up. They're valuable because the places they disagree mark exactly where the problem is genuinely hard. Where you are: you already use the tools, and what you get out looks like what everyone else gets out of the same ones.
q: Where all three agree, adding a person adds nothing.
The human value sits in the few moves where they disagree.

chapters.n: He spent years arguing the match didn't count
chapters.w: Conceding is cheaper than appealing
chapters.dek: What the first year after being replaced usually looks like. What he did, and what he said twenty years later.
chapters.txt: After the loss he told the press that IBM had used human intervention mid-match, and demanded a rematch. IBM refused, and dismantled Deep Blue — leaving him without even an opponent to play again. He told that version for years. By the time he wrote Deep Thinking in 2017 he had withdrawn it himself: Deep Blue won, and that is all. The 1997 explanations were what he couldn't accept at the time. Appealing and moving on can't run in parallel — The effort to prove that match didn't count and the effort to work out what to train next come out of the same person in the same stretch of time. The first buys no new skill even when it wins. The other side isn't waiting for your post-mortem — IBM dismantled the machine, which shows the pattern: whatever replaced you doesn't need your agreement and won't hold a rematch open for you. Hoping to end this by getting the other side to concede is usually a wait with no end. Conceding isn't surrendering — The same year he accepted the loss he was staging a tournament under new rules. Accepting a result and giving up the craft are two different things — accepting it first is what freed his hands to change the track. Nobody swallowing their pride changes anything. Where you are: a tool or a new method has beaten you, and most of your energy is going into explaining that it's unfair or that it isn't actually good. Ask first: how many times this month have I
q: Whatever replaced you does not need your agreement.
Proving it didn't count and deciding what to train next cost the same hours.

chapters.n: Ninety per cent of the time, thinking about failure
chapters.w: Think about losing before winning
chapters.dek: The richest man in Hong Kong describes his own split of attention, and it is not what you'd expect.
chapters.txt: In interviews Li Ka-shing has been blunt about it: ninety per cent of my time I spend considering failure. His image is a mechanical watch — one gear slightly faulty and the whole watch stops, and a company is the same. From his plastic-flowers days the habit was set: before a project starts, work through the ways it can fail. When success comes it needs very little thinking about. Beside it runs his rule on cash: a company can go bankrupt while profitable. Through decades of expansion his gearing stayed low. Rehearsing failure is insurance on the decision — Ninety per cent on failure isn't pessimism, it's a division of labour: failure modes are finite, listable and preventable. Having gone through each and set a gate, you can spend the remaining tenth committing hard. Optimism without that step stakes the company on luck. Find the gear that stops the whole watch — The watch image is precise about 'one gear'. What sinks a company is often not the main business but some unremarkable connector — a guarantee given, a maturity mismatch, one key person. So rank risks by whether they stop the watch, not by how big the business is. Cash flow is the floor under every failure case — Every rehearsed way of dying converges on the same place: is there enough in the account to get through. So his answer isn't don't take risks. It's make sure no single failure can cut the cash. Low debt isn't caution. It buys more chances to be wrong. Where you are:
q: Ninety per cent of my time, I spend considering failure.
One gear with the slightest fault and the watch stops.

chapters.n: Knowing where to stop
chapters.w: The two characters on his office wall
chapters.dek: A businessman famous for expansion looks up at a scroll telling him to stop. Stopping and not daring aren't the same.
chapters.txt: Li Ka-shing's office carries a scroll with two characters usually read as 'know where to stop', from a classical line: know where to stop and then you can be settled. Alongside it is the principle he repeats: never forget stability while growing, never forget growth while stable. In practice that meant selling down in overheated property, and walking away when a bid passed his line — moves others read as missing the market. He hung that scroll during Cheung Kong's most aggressive expansion. The faster you accelerate, the more you need a brake pad in permanent view. Write the stop before you sit down at the table — In practice this means writing the exit condition before every entry: above this price we don't chase, past this amount we don't add, at this date we don't renew. Written while unemotional, it needs no heroism to execute. Recalculating 'is it worth it' in the room is calculating your pride. What stops is the exposure, not the ambition — This gets misread as contentment with a little. His record says the opposite — decades from plastics to property to ports to telecoms, the ambition never paused. What was capped was the exposure of any single bet. Aggressive on direction, limited per bet: the second is what keeps the first alive. Hang the brake pad where you see it daily — Framing those two characters on the office wall is mechanism design. This is the string that goes first when things are going well, so the reminder has to be physically present —
q: Know where to stop, and then you can be settled.
Never forget stability while growing; never forget growth while stable.

chapters.n: Burnout has three parts. Tired is one
chapters.w: The other two warn you earlier
chapters.dek: Tired and burnt out are not the same thing. The three measures Maslach used to separate them.
chapters.txt: In 1981 Maslach built an inventory that split burnout into three components: emotional exhaustion (drained in a way sleep doesn't repair), depersonalisation (you start handling people as items, and can't summon interest in any of them), and a fall in personal accomplishment (nothing you do feels like it matters). Only the first overlaps with being tired. So somebody can look like they're working normally and still be delivering, while the other two have been running for months. Detachment warns earlier than exhaustion, and gets misread — Rest fixes tired. It does not fix detachment. Detachment looks like having nothing for colleagues, customers or family, and speech going formulaic. Others read it as someone turning cold; the person reads it as their personality changing. It's the second measure lighting up. 'I'm useless' isn't modesty, it's a reading — The third component is accomplishment collapsing: the same work finished, and where there used to be a little satisfaction there is now nothing. It gets treated as an attitude problem. On the inventory it is as measurable as the other two. They don't arrive together, so don't wait for the set — For most people detachment comes first, then exhaustion, and accomplishment collapses last. By the time all three are present, recovery takes far longer than it would have when one appeared. One of the three is enough to take seriously. Where you are: you suspect you're burnt out and keep telling yourself it's just tiredness. Ask first: which of the three do I have — drained, nothing left for people, no satisfaction
q: Sleep fixes tired. It does not fix detachment.
Still working normally and still delivering proves nothing about the other two.

chapters.n: Fix the job, not the person
chapters.w: Teaching people to relax repairs the wrong thing
chapters.dek: What to do about burnout. The mainstream answer may have the whole thing backwards, and she says why.
chapters.txt: The moment burnout was named, the market's fix became teaching people to relax: mindfulness, time management, resilience training. Maslach has argued against that direction for decades. Her claim is blunt: burnout is a problem of the work environment, not of individual resilience. Spending the effort on remaking the individual asks the person absorbing the damage to repair the thing causing it — and carries a second message along with it: if you can't take this, you aren't strong enough. Putting the responsibility in the wrong place makes it worse — Tell someone the problem is their attitude and they add a layer of self-blame, then stay in the same environment. The two together are much harder to climb out of than the exhaustion was on its own. Personal fixes aren't useless, they're second — Maslach never said sleep and exercise don't work. She said the order matters: see what in the working conditions can change, then talk about personal regulation. Reverse the order and personal regulation stops being support and starts being cover. For an individual, this means check the environment first — You may not be able to change the company, but you can do the accounting: is it too much work, or no say, or work that runs against what you care about? Each diagnosis points at a completely different move — what to negotiate, what to leave, what to refuse. Where you are: you're close to done, and everyone advises you to adjust your mindset and rest more. Ask first: if I took a month off, would
q: Asking the person absorbing the damage to repair its cause is backwards.
A mindfulness course and an unchanged rota send everyone back to the same schedule.

chapters.n: Six ways to be mismatched
chapters.w: Workload is only the first
chapters.dek: Same hours, and one person breaks while another doesn't. The six places she found the mismatch.
chapters.txt: Maslach and Leiter split the sources of burnout into six areas — the places where a person and a job fail to match: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Most people watch only the first. In her data the later ones are often more lethal, particularly having no say (control) and doing work that runs against what you believe (values). At identical hours, people matched on all six rarely break; people short two or three break quickly. Little work with no control hurts more than lots with control — Control is the second area and the most underrated. Few tasks, each needing sign-off and liable to be overturned at any moment, costs far more than a heavy load you get to arrange yourself. This matches what the stress research found independently. A values mismatch is the slowest and the deepest — The sixth area is doing work that runs against what you care about. It doesn't strike the same day; it hollows out the meaning gradually — the longer you do it the emptier it gets, and the less you can say why. Fix the other five and this one still takes you down. Score them separately or you can't tell what to move — 'Work is exhausting' implies no action at all. Score the six one by one and the answer usually gets specific: what you need to fight for is decision rights, or what you need to raise is fairness, or what you need is different work. Where you are: you can't say what is draining you,
q: Little work needing sign-off costs more than lots you decide yourself.
A values mismatch doesn't strike today. It hollows the meaning out slowly.

chapters.n: Change the environment before the behaviour
chapters.w: Out of reach is what looks like defiance
chapters.dek: Children considered unmanageable changed when the room changed. What was it that actually changed?
chapters.txt: In a poor district of Rome, Montessori did something then considered absurd: child-sized furniture, tools a child could work alone, children choosing their own activity, adults stepping in only when needed. Three- to six-year-olds thought unmanageable began repeating an activity for tens of minutes and tidying up afterwards. She called the state normalisation, and drew the foundation of the whole method: a child's work isn't taught into them; it happens in a prepared environment. Check whether the environment matches — A cup out of reach, a tool only an adult can operate — these manufacture dependence and frustration. Change the environment so the child can finish alone and the behaviour problem often disappears. It holds for adults too: plenty of self-discipline problems are environment problems. Concentration grows, it isn't demanded — She saw children concentrate for a long time on self-chosen work and lose focus quickly on assigned tasks. So the route to concentration is offering attractive choices and not interrupting — and the most common interruption is an adult's well-meant attention. The adult steps back into observer — This method asks more of the adult than the child: hold back from directing, from doing it for them, from prompting early. Montessori required teachers to learn observation first — see where the child is stuck and what they need, rather than pushing a plan along. Where you are: your child repeatedly can't do something and saying it again hasn't helped. Ask first: at their height, with their grip, with these tools — is it actually possible? Which single thing in
q: A child's work isn't taught in. It happens in a prepared room.
Education is not what the teacher said. It's what the child did.

chapters.n: Help me to do it myself
chapters.w: Doing it for them saves your time
chapters.dek: Doing it for them takes two minutes. What those two minutes bought, and what they cost.
chapters.txt: Montessori compressed the whole method into a child's request: help me to do it myself. That draws the boundary of help — the goal is that they can finish alone, not that the task finishes sooner. What an adult saves by taking over is their own time; what is spent is that one chance to learn. She also described sensitive periods: stages when a child absorbs a particular capacity with almost no effort. Hit the window and it is nearly free. Miss it and the same thing costs several times as much. Lower the difficulty to just within reach — The right intervention is neither taking over nor leaving them to it. It's adjusting the difficulty: break the task to a step they can do now and leave that step to them. It's the same thing deliberate practice calls the edge of the comfort zone, happening at three. Sensitive periods: wrong timing doubles the work — At two, a child is intensely sensitive to order, and habits of putting things away form easily. Try to establish the same rule at seven and the difficulty is completely different. Reading which period they're in beats working from an age chart. Slow is a cost and an investment — Letting a child do it will be slower and messier. Accepting that cost requires a longer time horizon: the ten extra minutes today buys years of not having to be involved. When the arithmetic doesn't get done, adults take over indefinitely. Where you are: they're slow and doing it badly and you can't stop
q: Help me to do it myself.
Every unnecessary help is an obstacle to development.

chapters.n: Invert, always invert
chapters.w: Study the ways it dies first
chapters.dek: He was asked how to have a good life and answered the other question instead. The swap is the whole method.
chapters.txt: Invited to address a graduating class, he announced he would explain how to guarantee a miserable life, and then worked through it: be unreliable, learn only from your own experience, go down when you take your first reverse, be consumed by envy and resentment. If you knew where you were going to die, he liked to say, you would simply never go there. The talk is the method demonstrated on itself, and it is more usable than any list of virtues he could have read out instead. One list is short and the other isn't — There are countless ways a thing can go well and a small number of ways it reliably goes wrong. The inverted question is simply a smaller problem, and a smaller problem is one you can actually finish. Failure modes are checkable; success stories aren't — You can go and look at whether the runway is short, whether one customer is half the revenue, whether the one person who understands the system is leaving. 'Is this a great idea' has no such test. It does not tell you what to do — Avoiding every failure mode leaves you alive, not successful. Inversion clears the ground; something still has to be built on it. Used alone it produces people who are very good at not losing and have not won anything. Where you are: about to commit to a plan you believe in. Ask first: spend twenty minutes writing only the ways this fails, then check how many are already true today. Where it goes wrong:
q: Invert, always invert.
If you knew where you were going to die, you would never go there.

chapters.n: One hammer is not enough
chapters.w: The danger is the skill, not the ignorance
chapters.dek: What he warned about was not ignorance. It was being very well trained in exactly one thing.
chapters.txt: At USC in 1994 he laid out the method of his life: you have to carry a number of models in your head and hang experience on that latticework. He put the count at eighty or ninety, drawn from mathematics, psychology, physics, biology and engineering. The warning attached to it is the line everyone knows: to a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail — and the man with the hammer is not the ignorant one, he is the well-trained one. The deeper the training, the better hidden the distortion — The hammer problem is not incompetence. It is that your discipline arrives with a viewfinder: the finance person sees a cost problem, the growth person a funnel problem. Each account is coherent, because any problem does have that face — and the coherence is what stops the search. Problems do not arrive by department — A pricing decision is economics and psychology and, because the competitor reacts, something close to biology. The latticework means laying several models over the same situation and seeing which one explains the most, rather than which one you already own. Load the models before you need them — A model you go and look up during the decision arrives too late to shape it. The models have to be in the head and automatic. There is no shortcut: take the two or three hardest ideas from each field and keep them. Where you are: diagnosing a problem inside your own speciality. Ask first: how would someone from a completely different
q: To a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.
The hammer man is not the ignorant one. He is the trained one.

chapters.n: Boil it down to what is physically true
chapters.w: Analogy quotes the going rate; physics gives the floor
chapters.dek: The phrase is everywhere now. What is worth having is his own definition, and the arithmetic he did on a battery.
chapters.txt: In the 2013 TED interview he set it out plainly: reason from first principles rather than by analogy. Analogy is everyone does it this way, so we will too. First principles is boiling a thing down to its most fundamental truths and reasoning up. His example was batteries. Everyone said a pack costs six hundred dollars a kilowatt-hour and always will. From first principles: what is a battery made of? Cobalt, nickel, aluminium, carbon, polymers, a steel can. Buy those on the metal exchange and it comes to eighty. The other five hundred is the price of how they are currently assembled — and assembly can be reinvented. Analogy gives you the market rate, physics gives the floor — It has always cost this and the industry standard both quote the price of other people's methods, not the cost of the thing. Separate the two: where is the floor set by materials and physical law, and who collects the gap between that floor and today's price? Keep going until you hit something that cannot be reduced — Most attempts stop halfway and treat a supplier quote or an industry convention as bedrock. Those are still somebody's decisions. The test is whether you can still ask why. If you can, you are not at the bottom. The bottom feels like a physical law or a published market price. It is expensive, so spend it where the leverage is — He has said himself that analogy is usually the cheaper move, and he is right: reasoning up the whole chain costs an
q: We reason from first principles rather than by analogy.
Boil things down to the most fundamental truths and reason up from there.

chapters.n: Part price over material price
chapters.w: A number that tells you where to start
chapters.dek: He gives every component a humiliating score. What it does is turn a way of thinking into something you can run on a spreadsheet.
chapters.txt: Isaacson records a hard metric inside SpaceX: the idiot index — the finished price of a part divided by the cost of its raw material. An aluminium part holding a few hundred dollars of metal, bought for tens of thousands, scores in the dozens. A score that absurd says what you are paying for is process and inertia, not physics. The rule follows: a high index is either explained or made in house. Many Falcon parts ended up built on site, at a fraction of the industry price. What makes the index good is that it turns a judgement call into a list you can sort. The index turns judgement into a scanner — First principles depends on someone deciding to think. The index makes the candidates queue up on their own: run the ratio across every purchased line, sort descending, and the rebuild priority list writes itself. The best form a method can take is decaying from an insight into a division anyone can do. A high score is a toll booth left by history — A part selling at fifty times its metal usually has no villain behind it: years of safety margin, layers of certification, small batches, a sole supplier. Every layer had a reason once; stacked up they are a row of toll booths. You do not negotiate those away, you route around them. Where the score is low, leave it alone — The tool carries its own limit. A part scoring near one is already priced against physics; making it yourself will not be cheaper,
q: The idiot index: a part's finished cost over its material cost.
A ratio that high means you are paying for process and inertia, not physics.

chapters.n: Assets that earn while you sleep
chapters.w: Wealth is not money
chapters.dek: The first line cuts one word into three. What matters is where each of the three leads.
chapters.txt: The storm opens: seek wealth, not money or status. Each is defined. Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep — businesses, code, content, equity. Money is how we transfer wealth. Status is your place in the social hierarchy. What matters is the kind of game each is. Creating wealth is positive sum: everyone can get richer. Status is zero sum — for you to rise somebody falls, which is why people attacking wealth creators are usually playing status. And there is one road to the first: ownership. You will not get rich renting out your time, because time does not copy. Work out which game you are actually playing — A great deal of hard work leads to status rather than wealth: titles, visibility, rankings. Those prizes produce no cash flow and require you to keep showing up to hold them. One test: stop for three months. Is it still producing? If yes it is an asset. Selling time has a ceiling because time will not copy — Work priced by the hour earns rate times hours. Both factors are hard-capped, and the whole thing goes to zero while you sleep. The way out is not raising the rate, it is changing the formula — detaching output from duration. Things made once and sold many times: code, content, courses, systems, equity. Recognising a status attack saves you the reply — Anyone who does something visible attracts a portion of criticism whose purpose is not correction but position — pushing you down in a zero-sum game. Separating the two kinds
q: Seek wealth, not money or status.
Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep.

chapters.n: Productise yourself
chapters.w: Specific knowledge times leverage
chapters.dek: He compresses the whole method into two words. What each of the two refers to, and why the new leverage is different in kind.
chapters.txt: The formula collapses into a phrase: productise yourself. Yourself means specific knowledge — the kind you cannot be trained for, growing out of your temperament, obsessions and history; it feels like play to you and looks like work to others. Productise means putting leverage on it. Labour and capital are the old kinds and both need somebody's permission. The new kind replicates at zero marginal cost: code and media, which need permission from nobody. What you wrote keeps working while you sleep. Specific knowledge is not on any syllabus — Any skill taught in a standard way is supplied in unlimited quantity and priced accordingly. Specific knowledge comes from the part that cannot be standardised: your combination of oddities, the crossings between fields, an obsession out of proportion to its subject. The detection method is his own line — play to you, labour to others. Permissionless means you can start today — The bottleneck in the old leverage is persuasion: nothing moves until you have hired someone or raised something. Code and media delete that step. Writing, recording, publishing — live today, at the cost of time rather than consent. The opportunity of this generation is essentially that the entry price of leverage fell to zero. Productising means taking yourself out of delivery — Where the two words end up: packaging your judgement, taste and method into something that delivers without you present. The test is replication — each additional user should cost you an amount of time approaching zero. Until then what you own is a good job. After
q: Productise yourself.
Specific knowledge feels like play to you but looks like work to others.

chapters.n: Do things that do not scale
chapters.w: The early work is meant to be handmade
chapters.dek: Founders think about scale constantly. He argues for the opposite direction — and is specific about what the handmade phase actually buys.
chapters.txt: The essay opens against the instinct: startups do not take off by themselves; the founders make them take off. The common mistake is chasing something scalable on day one, when the early period calls for recruiting users by hand. Airbnb had stalled, so the founders flew to New York week after week, knocked on hosts' doors and photographed their apartments themselves. Completely unscalable — and it found the switch that moved conversion. The output of that phase is not the handful of users; it is an unusually concentrated understanding of them, plus people so over-served they will tell others. Doing it by hand is the highest-bandwidth research there is — Surveys and dashboards show the shadow a behaviour casts; being in the room shows the behaviour. In people's living rooms it turned out photograph quality was the bottleneck — an insight the analytics could only ever have shown as low conversion. The expensive thing early on is not slow growth, it is understanding wrongly. Over-serving is how you manufacture the first advocates — If early users get service indistinguishable from a large company's, they have no reason to speak about you. The handmade phase gives what no scaled operation could — a founder replying in minutes, the product bent around one person. That unreasonable care is the raw material of word of mouth. Unscalable is a stage, not a creed — The essay gets quoted in halves. The correct loop is: do it by hand, extract the one move that was actually doing the work, then build that move into
q: Startups do not take off by themselves. The founders make them take off.
In the early days you have to recruit users manually.

chapters.n: Default alive or default dead
chapters.w: Run this number before anything else
chapters.dek: He asks founders one question first, and most of them cannot answer it. Why it comes before every other conversation.
chapters.txt: The first thing he asks a startup is are you default alive or default dead? The definition is hard-edged: assuming expenses stay constant and growth continues as it has been, do you reach profitability on the money you have left? If yes, default alive. If no, default dead. What surprised him is how many founders do not know which they are. It comes first because it sets the character of every other conversation: a default alive company can talk about ambition; a default dead one has a single agenda item, getting out of that state — and is usually still discussing hiring, assuming the next round will arrive. You have to run it yourself, because nothing raises an alarm — A default dead company looks entirely normal from inside: the product ships, the team grows, there is money in the account. Death is scheduled months out on a calendar nobody turns to. The question brings that date forward to today — three numbers, ten minutes. Counting on the next round outsources your survival to a mood — He names the standard consolation: investor appetite swings with the market and your death date does not. The right move when default dead is not to fundraise harder but to move the two variables under your control — expenses and growth — until you are back on the living side. The usual cause is hiring too early — His first-named cause of default dead is over-hiring — using growth needs people to raise the burn ahead of growth that then does not arrive.
q: Are you default alive or default dead?
With expenses flat and growth as it is, do you reach profitability in time?

chapters.n: Security and desire want opposite things
chapters.w: Which is why the better it gets, the flatter
chapters.dek: The steadier life gets, the less you feel, and most people assume they changed. Perel says the structure did it.
chapters.txt: Perel has done couples therapy for over thirty years, and the sentence she hears most is: everything is fine, we just don't feel anything. Her explanation blames nobody. Intimacy wants closeness, familiarity and predictability; desire wants distance, the unknown, the thing not yet fully held. Both are real needs and they point in opposite directions. So the more settled a relationship, the more easily the second gets squeezed out — not love going wrong, but one thing perfected until it crowds out the other. It isn't love fading. Two needs are crowding each other — Read as love fading, the only available moves are blaming yourself or blaming them. Read as two needs crowding, the move is clear: not repairing the love, but making room again for the one that got squeezed out. Familiar to the point of no unknown leaves nothing to miss — Desire needs a little opacity. When their schedule, thoughts and reactions are all inside your predictions, missing them has nowhere to land. So the problem often isn't too little communication — it's everything being accounted for. Room comes from separateness, not more closeness — The instinct is more time together, more talking. Perel's prescription often runs the other way: each go and do something the other isn't part of, become two people again, then come back. Distance isn't the enemy of love. It's the fuel of desire. Where you are: no fights, no crisis, and no feeling, and you can't say what's wrong. Ask first: when did we last each do something separately and come
q: Intimacy wants closeness. Desire wants distance. Both are real.
'Everything's fine, we feel nothing' says nothing about love failing.

chapters.n: Feeling nothing isn't the same as something being wrong
chapters.w: First tell a wound from an emptiness
chapters.dek: 'We can't go on like this' can sit on top of two completely different things. Tell them apart before you act.
chapters.txt: Perel warns about a common misdiagnosis: treating flatness as if it were rupture. Rupture has a wound — contempt, betrayal, sustained attack — and that needs mending. Flatness has no wound; it is simply empty, and emptiness needs filling, not mending. The two moves point in opposite directions: mending a wound means stopping first, apologising first, making it safe first; filling an emptiness means going outward and adding something new. Get it wrong and it worsens — apologising when you should be adding, booking trips when you should be apologising. Check for a wound before choosing a move — The test is concrete: in the last three months, has there been contempt, dragging up old grievances, belittling in front of others? If yes, that's the wound and it comes first. If none of it, this is emptiness, and the treatment is entirely different. For emptiness, more communication makes it worse — Repeatedly sitting down to discuss the relationship when it's empty talks away the last of the ease. What it needs is experiencing something new together, not analysing why there's no feeling — the analysis itself turns the relationship into a task. Only after telling them apart is 'should we leave' answerable — People decide about leaving while the two states are mixed together, so the answer keeps swinging. See first whether it's a wound or an emptiness, then ask — the answers under those two premises were never meant to match. Where you are: you don't fight and you aren't close, and you're weighing mending against leaving. Ask first:
q: A wound is mended, an emptiness is filled. Opposite directions.
Talking it through while empty talks away the last of the ease.

chapters.n: It isn't how often. It's not being there
chapters.w: Present in the room, absent in attention
chapters.dek: You live in the same place. So why does it feel like long distance? What she says to count instead.
chapters.txt: Most people count time: how many evenings a week, how many meals together. Perel says that's the wrong ledger — what decides the quality isn't how long you're together but how many moments both people were actually there. Two people on the same sofa on separate phones have spent a whole evening together and zero minutes present. She asks clients something very concrete: when did you last look at each other and talk with no screen interrupting? Count 'together' and 'present' separately — They're different ledgers: together is duration, present is attention. The first stacks up easily; the second can be zero for a whole week. What makes someone feel loved is the second, and it has almost nothing to do with the first. Presence can be practised, and it's cheap — It doesn't need large blocks of time: fifteen minutes a day, person facing person, phones face down, is enough to change how it feels. The difficulty isn't the duration, it's not glancing away — one break and that stretch is over. Long enough absent and it reads as not caring — They don't know what your head is busy with. All they can read is where your attention goes, and from that, where they rank. So sustained distraction doesn't communicate 'I'm busy'. It communicates 'you're not important'. Where you are: you're together every day and drifting further apart. Ask first: when did I last look at them and talk without touching my phone? If you can't name the day, start there before discussing the relationship. Where it goes
q: Together counts duration. Present counts attention.
Same sofa, separate phones: zero minutes present.

chapters.n: Forty years of sitting the exam
chapters.w: Never passing, and never a turning point
chapters.dek: There's a kind of failure with no decisive battle in it. How you get through that kind of life.
chapters.txt: At nineteen Pu Songling sat the entry examinations and came first at county, prefecture and circuit level. He was locally famous. Then he sat the provincial examination for the rest of his life, from his twenties into his sixties, and never once passed, supporting his family as a live-in tutor. At seventy-one he was granted a minor honorary status by seniority. No single year in all of it was decisive — not one big defeat and a restart, but once every three years, each time just short, until he was old. Failure with no turning point is the hardest kind — Lose a battle and you can review it and change direction. Forty years of being just short offers no single event worth reviewing and no signal about whether to stop. Most advice about handling failure assumes there is a turning point to point at. Here there isn't one. He didn't stop, and he didn't make it everything — Worth noticing: he neither gave up the exam nor staked the whole of his life on it. The tutoring continued, the family was kept, the stories were collected. Running them in parallel means that when the thing that never worked fails again, something else in your hands is working. You may keep more than one ruler — The examination was a ruler handed to him from outside, clear and unambiguous — which is exactly what makes it easy to let it become the only one. He had a second: how many stories this year. The second doesn't make the first easier.
q: No year was decisive. Just short every time, until he was old.
A lost battle can be reviewed. Being just short cannot.

chapters.n: The main thing failed. The side thing didn't
chapters.w: And he never knew
chapters.dek: What he spent his life trying to do never happened. What he did on the side did. Can that be arranged?
chapters.txt: Pu Songling's real work, as he saw it, was the examination. Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio was a diversion — forty years of writing, circulated in manuscript among friends, and he did not live to see it printed. Of the people who remember him today, essentially none do so for his examination essays. The thing ranked first didn't happen and the thing ranked last did — and he died not knowing it. You don't get to set the ranking — Where a thing sits in your own ordering and what it eventually grows into are unrelated. The first is decided by today's standards; the second takes decades to show. So 'which is the main thing' is a question that, asked at the time, usually gets the wrong answer. But don't therefore do both casually — Strange Tales wasn't written carelessly — forty years, nearly five hundred pieces, revised repeatedly. It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment. A side thing can only grow into something if it gets real investment; it just doesn't get the status. Don't wait until you approve of it to take it seriously — He never considered it his achievement. If you have to wait until you can admit 'this is my real work' before putting the hours in, a great many things simply never grow. The steadier practice is to work seriously and leave the ranking undecided. Where you are: your day job is flat and the thing you do in the evenings keeps growing, and you don't know whether to
q: The thing ranked first failed. The thing ranked last didn't.
It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment.

chapters.n: Collecting stories by the road
chapters.w: Using the hours nobody wants
chapters.dek: Forty years of a tutor's scattered hours. What he did with them, and how the material accumulated.
chapters.txt: There is a persistent account that Pu Songling set out tea by the roadside and asked passers-by for strange stories, waiving the price of a bowl for each one, then wrote them up at home. It comes from later writers, not from him, and may not be literal. But it matches a checkable fact: he spent forty years as a live-in tutor in gentry households, with a great deal of scattered time around the teaching, and the nearly five hundred pieces accumulated across exactly those years. He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job. Accumulation needs somewhere fixed for things to land — Scattered hours turn into something not because there are many of them but because there is one fixed place that catches them. A thing overheard, a sentence that occurs to you — all into the same notebook. Without that catch, the same forty years simply disperse. The material is local. You don't go far for it — His sources were the ordinary talk of villagers in the county he tutored in, not the fruit of travels through famous mountains. What's genuinely scarce isn't remarkable experience. It's the eye that treats what's around you as material — most people have as much of it and aren't collecting. Not quitting is what let it run so long — The tutoring fed him and gave him forty uninterrupted years. Had he staked everything on writing, he probably couldn't have lasted. What kills a side project isn't too little investment. It's gambling your living alongside it and
q: He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job.
Scattered hours add up because something catches them, not because there are many.

chapters.n: Swap the cage for a park
chapters.w: Same rat, different situation
chapters.dek: The most famous addiction experiment gave a conclusion against intuition. What happens when you change the cage.
chapters.txt: The standard 1970s addiction experiment went like this: put one rat alone in an empty cage with two bottles, one water and one laced with morphine. The rat drinks the morphine until it dies. The conclusion looks solid — touch it once and you're finished. Bruce Alexander in Canada asked a different question: what if the cage weren't empty? He built a much larger enclosure with companions, wheels, tunnels and places to hide. Same two bottles, and the rats in the park were far less interested in the morphine. The variable isn't only the bottle. It's the cage — The original design treated the cage as background and the drug as the only variable. Once Alexander made the cage a variable too, the conclusion moved: same rat, same bottle, different situation, very different behaviour. The drug's effect isn't denied. It just isn't the only term. The empty cage is manufacturing the demand — The park rats weren't restrained; they didn't much want it. Alexander later used the word dislocation: pull an individual out of the relationships and position they belong in and they will look for anything that fills the gap. The gap is what's being filled. This has a boundary, and it has to be stated — Rat Park's replications were not uniformly successful and its interpretation is still argued over. The safe reading is that situation is the chronically underrated term, not the only one. Explaining everything with it delays people who need medical care. Where you are: you want to stop something — the phone, drinking, whatever
q: Same rat, same bottle. Different cage, different behaviour.
They weren't holding out. They didn't much want it.

chapters.n: Back home, most of them simply stopped
chapters.w: The hardest natural experiment there is
chapters.dek: Is there harder evidence than rats? What the numbers on returning soldiers actually showed.
chapters.txt: In 1971 the US government discovered an awkward problem: a substantial proportion of American servicemen in Vietnam were addicted to heroin. Everyone braced for a disaster — these men would carry it home into the cities. Robins's team followed them and found the opposite. The overwhelming majority simply stopped once home, with only a small fraction relapsing within a year. Same people, same drug, different place. It is one of the very few natural experiments in addiction research with a sample this size. Its strength is that nobody designed it — Laboratory findings always carry the worry that they were engineered. This one wasn't — nobody sent hundreds of thousands of people to a war and brought them back in order to prove a point. Not being designed is exactly what makes it more persuasive than any experiment. What changed wasn't the place. It was the whole situation — Coming home swapped out an entire set of conditions: no longer possibly dying at any moment, family instead of fellow soldiers, a job and a schedule, and the substance much harder to get. So changing environment isn't moving house. It's withdrawing the conditions holding it up. The fraction who relapsed says something else — Some did continue after returning. That fraction is the reminder: situation explains the bulk, not all of it. Who lands in it has more to do with what home was like and what else was going on than with the drug. Where you are: you're trying to help yourself or a family member stop something, and you've
q: Same people, same substance. Home again, and they stopped.
The weight of this data is that nobody designed it.

chapters.n: Take the cage apart before the willpower
chapters.w: And where this stops being true
chapters.dek: Once you know the situation matters, what exactly do you move? How to take the cage apart one bar at a time.
chapters.txt: Put the last two pieces together and you get a method that runs against common sense: to stop something, don't fight the thing itself first. Look at what keeps it alive. A habit that lasts usually has a whole set of props — a fixed hour, a fixed place, nothing else to hand, people doing it with you. Withdraw those one at a time and the thing gets harder by itself, whereas fighting it head-on withdraws only your willpower, which is the first thing to run out. Keep the log before you move anything — Log ten in a row: the hour, the place, whether anything else was in your hands, who was there. Most people finish the log and find the trigger isn't craving, it's one recurring empty slot. Finding the slot is worth more than studying how to resist. Whatever replaces it has to actually work — Removing something leaves a gap, and a gap gets filled back the same way. What worked in Rat Park wasn't the absence of morphine, it was companions, wheels, somewhere to go. So the second step is putting something you genuinely like into that slot, not leaving it bare. When the cage can't be moved, this doesn't apply — The method assumes the cage is movable. Some situations aren't — you can't leave the job, move the family, replace the person. Forcing 'change your environment' there only adds a layer of failure. That's when to find professional help rather than keep pushing on the situation. Where you are: you want to stop
q: Take apart the props holding it up, not the thing itself.
The trigger is often not craving. It's one recurring empty slot.

chapters.n: Built for escape, left switched on
chapters.w: The problem is that it won't turn off
chapters.dek: People and zebras run the same stress system. Why only one of them gets sick from it.
chapters.txt: The title is the whole argument. Zebras don't get ulcers because their stress response runs for a few minutes. A lion charges: heart rate up, glucose released, immune function paused — and the moment they've escaped, it shuts off. Ours is identical, and we run it against mortgages, managers and an unanswered email. So Sapolsky's verdict is that what makes people ill isn't the stress, it's the response staying on. Its price is suspended repair, digestion and long-term building. Fine briefly. Left on, it diverts the maintenance budget indefinitely. It isn't intensity, it's duration — A week-long sprint doesn't damage anyone. Two years of being permanently on call does. To assess your own state, the question isn't how tired you've been lately. It's when the system was last genuinely switched off. The cost is charged somewhere you can't see — What gets paused under stress is immunity, digestion and tissue repair, and those debts don't show up the same day. So people misjudge how well they're coping. By the time symptoms appear the account has usually been running a long while. The specifically human problem is imagination — A zebra starts the response on seeing an actual lion. A person can start the entire thing by thinking about something that might happen. That's the core mechanism of chronic human stress, and why working on the thoughts themselves is a real intervention. Where you are: tense for a long time, unable to point at what's wrong. Ask first: when did this system last actually switch off? Has there been any stretch
q: Zebras don't get ulcers because the response runs for minutes.
What makes people ill is the response that won't switch off.

chapters.n: Uncertainty hurts more than intensity
chapters.w: Predictability and control
chapters.dek: Same pressure, and one person breaks while another doesn't. What the actual variable turns out to be.
chapters.txt: Sapolsky spent thirty years watching wild baboons in East Africa. Low-ranking animals ran chronically high stress hormones and worse health across the board. But rank wasn't the key thing: at the same low rank, individuals who could anticipate when they'd be harassed, and who had social allies, had markedly better markers. The lab agrees. At the same pressure, predictability and a sense of control cut the damage sharply. That moves the intervention from reducing stress to adding certainty and autonomy — usually far cheaper. Definite bad news beats being left hanging — People and animals adapt to a certain bad. They don't adapt to uncertainty. Which is why delaying an announcement often does more harm than the announcement — for the whole delay, everyone is on call. Control is a cheap buffer — At identical workload, people who decide their own order and pace show a markedly lower stress response. Adding autonomy doesn't require removing any tasks and cuts the wear substantially. Social support is a physiological variable — Baboons with allies, and people with stable relationships, show better markers under equal pressure. This isn't reassurance, it's a measurable difference. Isolation is itself a health risk. Where you are: under heavy pressure that isn't going to decrease. Ask first: is there any way to make what's coming more predictable — a fixed date, a definite answer? Can I take back some say over the order and pace? Where it goes wrong: turning 'control helps' into needing to control everything, which is a new load of its own.
q: Same pressure. With predictability and control, far less damage.
Low-ranking baboons ran high hormones. The ones with allies didn't.

chapters.n: No wind, no rain, no sun
chapters.w: Switching off the scoring
chapters.dek: Everyone else on the road was miserable. He was not. What exactly did he switch off in that moment?
chapters.txt: In 1082 Su Shi — a Song poet two years into exile, recently released from a prison that nearly killed him — was caught in rain on a country road. The servant with the rain gear had gone ahead. Everyone was wretched; he wasn't. When it stopped he wrote a short poem. It ends by looking back at the road he had just walked: there had been no wind, no rain, and no sun either. Wretched is a verdict, not a fact — Same rain, same road. The difference isn't who got wet. It's who filed the afternoon under 'this is going badly.' Misery needs a scoring system to exist. Switch that off and what's left is water hitting you. Why not walk slowly — The rain gear is gone. Walking faster gets you marginally less wet and costs you the walk. His line isn't bravado; it's arithmetic: don't spend more of yourself accelerating through the part you can't change. The last line is the hard one — 'No wind, no rain, no sun' doesn't claim it never rained. It says that from far enough along the road, neither the storm nor the sun is an event. That view is only true afterwards — which is why it's worth borrowing early. Where you are: something bad is settled and you keep replaying it. Ask first: is the pain the thing itself, or the frame I keep putting around it? Where it goes wrong: reading this as permission not to deal with the problem, or using 'this too shall pass' to
q: Don't listen to the rain in the leaves. Walk on, and hum.
Looking back at that bleak road — no wind, no rain, no sun.

chapters.n: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou
chapters.w: Doing real work where you were sent to rot
chapters.dek: Asked at the end of his life to name what he'd accomplished, he named three places he'd been banished to. Why those?
chapters.txt: A year before he died, Su Shi saw a portrait of himself in a temple and wrote a few lines under it. He had been a Hanlin academician and a minister of rites. He listed none of that. Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou — his three places of exile, each further from the capital than the last, the third on a tropical island then considered the edge of the world. Treat the exile as a term in office — Sent somewhere with no resources and no future, most people wait it out. He treated each posting as a term: what does this place most lack, and what can I leave behind. Rank sets your authority, not whether you work. Leave things somebody can point at — A lake dredged and a causeway built. A society to stop infant drowning. A public clinic. A school on an island that had never produced a scholar. Abstract achievements evaporate when the scoring changes; objects stay. He set the measure himself — By the official ledger his career was the titles. By listing three places of banishment he announced that the ruler measuring his life was in his own hand. That isn't consolation. It's taking the scorekeeping back. Where you are: you've been put somewhere with no resources and no prospects. Ask first: what does this place most lack right now, and what could I leave behind that someone could point at? Where it goes wrong: treating endurance as a strategy; scoring yourself in titles instead of finished things.
q: Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou.
While I am here, the water will not take this city.

chapters.n: I see no bad people
chapters.w: Treating a person as a person
chapters.dek: A man whose enemies nearly had him executed said he could see no bad people anywhere. This is not naivety.
chapters.txt: Su Shi was jailed over lines from his own poems and came close to execution. For twenty years afterwards, as two factions traded power, he was demoted again and again — the last time to a tropical island. He opposed the reformers' new laws, then opposed the conservatives when they scrapped every one of them. Neither side could keep him. Late in life he told his brother: I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar. I see no bad people. Refusing to sort people into sides — Faction logic labels the person first and lets the label decide every interaction after. He judged each measure on its merits and was exiled by both sides for it. Not neutrality — a refusal to use the frame. 'Bad person' is an expensive verdict — Once you decide someone is bad, your available moves collapse to guarding and fighting, and both burn enormous amounts of you. Seeing a person with their own situation and interests is what lets you work the actual disagreement. This is not the same as having no judgement — He knew exactly who was working against him, and knew his own mouth was the danger. 'No bad people' describes how he treated people, not how he assessed them. Confuse the two and you become either a pushover or a cynic. Where you are: there's history with someone, and now every contact is defensive. Ask first: if I treat him as a person with his own situation, can this specific disagreement be discussed? Where it goes wrong:
q: I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar.
I see no bad people.

chapters.n: Clear the ground first
chapters.w: The first thing he did when the salary stopped
chapters.dek: Exiled to Huangzhou, his salary essentially gone. The first thing he did was not write poetry.
chapters.txt: In 1080 Su Shi arrived in Huangzhou holding an empty title, barred from official business, with almost no income and twenty-odd people to feed. What he did first was unglamorous: he petitioned for an abandoned military plot east of town — fifty acres of scrub hillside, which he and his family broke themselves — and planted wheat and rice, dug a well, built a house. 'East Slope' is not a poetic sobriquet. It's the name of the field. The poems came after the ground did. Solve eating before you solve meaning — When income stops, the easiest thing to do is work out what this means about you. His order was the reverse: get this month and next year fed, and put the rest later. Not a refusal to think — thinking done hungry doesn't count anyway. He also kept a ledger — Arriving in Huangzhou he split what money was left into thirty portions and hung them from a beam, taking one a day and saving the remainder in a tube for guests. The point isn't the amount. It's that 'how long can I last' became a number he could see. What you make gives you a place to stand — The field produced more than grain: it produced a name. He stopped being a demoted official and became the layman of East Slope. When the old position is taken, finishing one concrete thing grows a new one faster than waiting to be recognised again. Where you are: the income has stopped, or is about to, and you're circling
q: Meaning arrived at while hungry mostly doesn't count.
When the old place is taken, finish one small thing.

chapters.n: The mud had to go somewhere
chapters.w: Turning the by-product into the thing
chapters.dek: Dredging a lake leaves you holding the mud. What he did with it is still there a thousand years later.
chapters.txt: By 1090 West Lake at Hangzhou was half weed and silt, and Su Shi, posted there as prefect, put twenty thousand men on clearing it. That solved one problem and created another: the spoil had to go somewhere, and carting it out of the city would have cost more than the dredging. He laid it across the water instead, as a causeway with six bridges. A walk that had taken most of a day around the shore became a short crossing. It still carries his name. The waste is only waste until you name a use — Nobody asked him to build a causeway; the job was to clear the lake. The mud became a road because he was willing to ask what else it could be, at the moment everyone else was asking where to dump it. Solve it where the work already is — He did not start a second project. The men, the boats and the spoil were already on the water — the causeway cost the difference between carting mud away and setting it down in a line. The real job came first — The causeway is what people remember, but the case he argued was for the lake: without it the farms lost their water, the canal silted, the brewing tax fell. The road was what the work left over, not the reason for it. Next time a job leaves you with something to get rid of — a half-finished draft, a dataset built for one question, a team freed up by a cancellation —
q: The spoil from the dredging is the causeway.
Everyone was asking where to dump it. He asked what it could be.

chapters.n: I dare not write
chapters.w: Stopping the defence is a decision
chapters.dek: After his own words were used to build a case against him, did he keep writing? The question is which kind he stopped.
chapters.txt: In the Crow Terrace case, Su Shi's poems were read line by line as evidence of slander against the throne. He spent over a hundred days in prison and nearly lost his life. Afterwards, in letter after letter to friends, the same sentence: I dare not write. It wasn't fear — he wrote his most famous work in those same years. What he stopped was a different thing: defending himself, arguing who was right. He kept the two clearly apart. You pay for the defence yourself — Arguing over who was right spends your hours and the other person's patience, and winning returns neither. Worse, it has no end: every reply earns another, unless somebody stops. Stopping isn't conceding. It's capping the cost. It's an action you can tell you took — 'Let it go' can't be executed — there's no way to know you've done it. 'I don't write that kind of thing anymore' can: next time your fingers move, you know what you're doing. A mood can't be kept. An action can. Know which kind stops and which continues — He stopped the defending, not the writing. The distinction matters: putting down the pen entirely is self-punishment and takes the real work with it. Only one kind should stop — the kind whose purpose is to make someone admit you were right. Where you are: you're being misread or blamed, you keep explaining, and it keeps getting worse. Ask first: is the next thing I write meant to make the facts clear, or to get someone to say
q: He stopped defending himself. He did not stop writing.
Every reply earns another, unless somebody stops.

chapters.n: Win first, then fight
chapters.w: The work happens before the clash
chapters.dek: Everyone quotes it as bravado. Read slowly it says the opposite: by the time you are fighting, it is mostly decided.
chapters.txt: The line is four characters longer in Chinese than in any translation, and it is built as a pair: the victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards, the defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards. It is not advice about how to fight. It is a claim about when the outcome is set. The book spends its early chapters on measurement — ground, numbers, supply, weather, the character of the commander — because that is where the decision actually happens. Preparation is not the same as planning — A plan is a description of what you intend to do. Preparation is changing the conditions until the intended thing becomes easy. The first can be done at a desk in an afternoon; the second takes months and shows up as very little visible activity. If it needs courage, something upstream went wrong — Reaching for nerve is usually the sign that the conditions were not set. Sometimes there is no choice. But treating courage as the plan converts an upstream failure into a personal one, and hides the part that could have been fixed. Not starting is a move — If the conditions are not there, the strongest available action is to not begin yet. This is the hardest part to practise, because waiting looks identical to doing nothing, and only one of them has a reason. Where you are: something is coming that you are bracing for. Ask first: what would have to already be true for this to go well? Write the list, and see
q: The victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards.
The defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards.

chapters.n: Know both, and know which is harder
chapters.w: Your own numbers are the flattered ones
chapters.dek: Quoted for two thousand years, usually as a case for research. The half everybody skips is the one about yourself.
chapters.txt: The Estimates chapter is not a maxim, it is a form to fill in: five dimensions and seven comparisons — whose ruler has the way, whose commanders are abler, who has the ground and the season, whose discipline is enforced, whose troops are stronger, whose are better drilled, whose rewards and punishments are clear. Then a coldly practical conclusion: if the count comes out favourable, fight; if it does not, don't. He called it reckoning in the temple — settle it before you decide whether to go at all. Knowing is a filled-in table, not an impression — 'I have a rough sense of the competition' is not knowing. The value of a list of comparisons is that it forces out the row you cannot answer, and the row you cannot answer is usually the one that decides it. Your own side is the harder half — Their information is outside you and can be gone and found. Yours has been through several people who each had a reason to round it kindly. The order in the sentence puts them first; the difficulty runs the other way. The count has to be allowed to say no — More reckoning wins, less reckoning loses. The point of the exercise is not to find a way to win; it is that it can output 'this one should not be fought'. A process that ends in action whatever it computes is not a decision, it is a ceremony. Where you are: about to commit to something competitive on the strength of a general
q: More reckoning wins. Less reckoning loses.
Theirs is outside and findable. Yours has been through people.

chapters.n: The best fight is the one nobody has
chapters.w: Winning a hundred times is not the top of the list
chapters.dek: A hundred victories sounds like the ceiling. He says it isn't, and the reason is arithmetic rather than modesty.
chapters.txt: The chapter gives a ranked list that runs against instinct: attack the enemy's plan first, his alliances second, his army third, and his walled cities last. Each step down costs more and returns less. On sieges he is unusually specific — three months to prepare the engines, three more for the ramps, and a commander who loses patience and sends men up the walls like ants, a third of them dead and the city still standing. He calls that the disaster of assault. Winning is also spending — A hundred victories is not the height of skill; subduing the enemy without fighting is. Every win costs people, money, time and trust. The side that won five times can easily be stronger than the side that won a hundred. Plan, then alliances, then force — Attacking the plan means making their approach stop making sense on its own terms. Attacking alliances means removing the support it rests on. Neither requires contact. By the time only fighting is left, the first two were skipped or botched. The most expensive move is the one you take personally — Assault happens when there is nothing else left, or when someone cannot stand to walk away. He singles out the commander who attacks in anger. Losing a third of your strength to a wall you did not need is a decision made by a mood. Where you are: locked into a fight you expect to win. Ask first: what does winning this cost, and what would have to be true for it not to be
q: Winning a hundred battles is not the height of skill.
Every win you take spends people, money, time and trust.

chapters.n: The flank only works if the front holds
chapters.w: A clever move on its own is a donation
chapters.dek: Everyone wants the unexpected move. The chapter is mostly about the unglamorous thing it has to stand on.
chapters.txt: The Energy chapter asks why the same troops behave like a rolling log one day and a scattered crowd the next. His answer is the pairing: engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary. The orthodox is the part that meets them head on and holds; the extraordinary is what comes from the side. He insists the two convert into each other endlessly — which means today's surprise, once used, becomes tomorrow's front. Without the front, the flank hits air — The surprise works because the other side is already gripped and cannot turn. Let the front go slack and the clever move lands on nothing, with your best people stranded out in the open. A surprise used once becomes the expected thing — Any unexpected move, once used and written up, enters the other side's expectations and becomes part of the front. Planning to live for years off one trick is spending a one-time resource as if it were income. Position, not heroics — The chapter ends not on cleverness but on structure: put the rock at the top of a thousand-foot mountain and the force of it coming down is not the rock's. Seek it in the position, and do not demand it of the people. Where you are: pinning your hopes on one inventive move. Ask first: what is holding the front while that move happens, and is it actually holding? Where it goes wrong: concluding that only the basics matter — the front alone defends and never wins.
q: Engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary.
Used once, the surprise becomes the thing they expect.

chapters.n: Take the shape of what you meet
chapters.w: Avoiding the strong part is the hard half
chapters.dek: 'Be like water' became a poster. The chapter is stricter than the poster, and most of it is about what not to do.
chapters.txt: The chapter is about who is setting the terms: bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him. Strike what he must defend and he has to come. Decline the engagement and he cannot force it. Then the image everybody knows: water has no constant shape, it avoids the heights and runs to the low ground, and an army has no constant form either — it avoids what is solid and strikes what is hollow. Having no fixed shape is the point — What water resembles is not softness, it is the absence of a preset form. Its shape is decided entirely by what it meets. Which makes 'what is our style of competing' a question with a flaw built into it. Avoiding the solid part is discipline, not opportunism — The hard half is the avoiding. The places that look most worth taking, most prestigious, most expected of you are usually exactly where they are thickest. Declining them means absorbing internal pressure, which is harder than spotting the gap. Who wrote this week's calendar — Initiative is not moving first. It is that the other side has to answer at your tempo. There is a simple test: look at the week you just had and ask whether you scheduled it, or whether their moves did. Where you are: reacting to a competitor, or defending the position you are proudest of. Ask first: where are they actually thin, and what would it cost you internally to walk away from the thick part? Where it goes wrong: using it
q: Bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him.
Water has no constant shape. That is what it is being praised for.

chapters.n: Whatever peaks, turns
chapters.w: The top is where to start worrying
chapters.dek: Usually read as comfort for bad times. It is more useful as an instrument, and it is sharpest when things are going well.
chapters.txt: Four characters: reversal is the movement of the way. The claim is not that things get better, nor that they get worse. It is that anything carried to its extreme starts producing its opposite. Which means the most dangerous moment is not the trough — it is the peak, because that is where nobody is looking for the turn. In the trough the rule is working for you and nothing needs to be done about it. Read it at the top, not at the bottom — In a bad stretch the line reads as reassurance and asks nothing of you. In a good stretch it asks a question you would rather not answer: which of the things carrying us right now is at full stretch, and what happens when it stops. Extremes, not durations — It says nothing about how long anything lasts. A thing at moderate stretch can run for decades. What turns is what has been pushed as far as it goes — margin at its thinnest, hours at their longest, patience at its end. The move is to give something back early — If the turn is structural, the cheap version is to stop short of the extreme on purpose: take some off the table, keep the slack, decline the last increment. The expensive version is to have it taken from you at the turn. Where you are: something is going unusually well and you are being asked to push it further. Ask first: what is at full stretch right now, and what breaks when it stops?
q: Reversal is the movement of the way.
The dangerous moment is the peak, because nobody is looking for the turn there.

chapters.n: The part you don't do
chapters.w: A list of moves to leave out
chapters.dek: Usually translated as non-action and read as passivity. It is closer to a list of the moves that make things worse.
chapters.txt: His verdict on governing is cold: the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people; the more laws are published, the more thieves there are. The alternative he offers is not letting go. It is: I do nothing and they transform themselves, I stay still and they correct themselves, I leave them alone and they prosper. The load-bearing word is themselves. The point is not to stop things happening; it is to stop being the thing that prevents them. Subtracting moves, not making none — In learning you gain daily; in the way you lose daily. Getting good at running something is largely removing the actions that look like management and function as interference. Take out enough and the thing moves on its own. There is a mechanism behind more rules, more problems — Every prohibition creates an incentive to route around it, and every correction leaves room for the next deviation. This is not a claim about morality; it is that a control grows the behaviour it was built to stop. Act while it is still small — Deal with the difficult while it is easy, the large while it is small. Non-action is not never acting — it is moving the action earlier, when a small one is enough. Wait and you need a large one, and large ones have consequences of their own. Where you are: about to add a rule, a process or a meeting to fix something. Ask first: which existing action is producing this problem, and what happens if you remove it instead? Where
q: The more laws are published, the more thieves there are.
Every prohibition creates a reason to route around it.

chapters.n: Go to the low ground
chapters.w: Not competing is a choice of location
chapters.dek: Water has been praised for two thousand years. The text credits it with one specific thing, and it is about position.
chapters.txt: He gives water two lines, and both are needed. It benefits all things without contending — and it settles in the places people find distasteful. The second is what makes the first possible: not contending is not a posture, it is a choice of site. He is blunter later — the reason the rivers and seas are king of the hundred valleys is that they are good at being below them. Things flow to you because you are lower. Not contending means standing where nobody is — The line is usually read as moral advice and is closer to geometry: if the position you are in is one nobody wants, the act of contending does not arise. It is settled at the siting stage, not in the fight. The places people find distasteful — Low competitive density hides in the work that is dirty, slow, or takes years to show a result. Those positions are empty precisely because they look bad and produce nothing reportable for a long time. Height stops the flow — If you want people, information or resources to come to you, you have to be positioned below them. This is most visible with information: the higher the posture, the less of what is actually happening reaches you. Where you are: choosing what to work on, in a space where everyone is going for the same thing. Ask first: which necessary job is empty because it looks unrewarding, and what would being there let you see? Where it goes wrong: mistaking it for accepting bad treatment —
q: It benefits all things without contending, and settles where people find distasteful.
The rivers rule the valleys by being below them.

chapters.n: The empty part is the useful part
chapters.w: What you left out is doing the work
chapters.dek: Which part of a wheel is doing the work? The chapter is short enough to be a definition and it underwrites the whole book.
